tagline.text: Biliran Island's highest peak, a two-day climb through waterfalls and mossy forest

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,000~3,500 (local costs for 2 days and 1 night, excluding flights and travel from Manila)

children.text: Mt. Tres Marias is the highest mountain on Biliran Island, a massif of three connected peaks. The overnight climb starts in Sampao, crosses waterfalls and streams, camps at Aeta Campsite, and reaches the summit the next morning. Philippine hikers rate it a demanding trail.

Mt. Tres Marias rises in the central highlands of Biliran Island, just north of Leyte. The name is Spanish for "Three Marias" and is said to come from its three peaks standing side by side. Hikers usually call Peak 1 Sugo, Peak 2 Naliwatan, and Peak 3 the main summit, which hiking sources give as the highest point on Biliran. Its height varies by source: the Philippine hiking blog Pinoy Mountaineer gives about 1,315 m, while the hiking app Akyat and the mountain database GunungBagging give 1,346 m. Either way, think of it as a mountain in the 1,300 m range.

The most common route starts in Sampao, Almeria, Biliran. You register at the village entrance, hire a guide, and begin walking. Along the way you pass Sampawan Falls first, then Ulan-Ulan Falls, Recoletos Falls, and Nomads Falls in turn. Past the waterfalls the trail follows a river, then climbs a steep, muddy slope to Aeta Campsite. Most groups leave for the summit early the next morning.

From around 1,200 m the forest turns mossy, and pitcher plants are reported near the top. The trail is rough and often wet, so Philippine hiking guides class it as a major climb, difficulty 5/9, trail class 2~4. Many people choose it as their first major climb, yet "the hardest hike I have done" is a common phrase in trip reports.

This entry is based on the standard summit climb. There are also programs run by some operators that cover the massif's three peaks over three to five days, plus canyoning on the Sampao River, but prices and schedules differ by operator, so confirm directly with them. Sources disagree on the exact summit coordinates. The coordinates here use the location given for Naliwatan, the highest peak, so treat them as an approximate position for the massif.

Being the island's highest point is the biggest draw. Looking down on dense forest and clouds from the summit is hard to match on a flat-land trip. Trip reports often note, however, that heavy fog can block the view.

blocks.title: A string of waterfalls early on

children.text: Reports usually single out Ulan-Ulan Falls as the most impressive, and it is said to photograph best when afternoon light hits it. Recoletos Falls and Nomads Falls have pools for swimming, which makes them good rest stops mid-climb.
Many stretches involve hopping across rocks or wading with wet shoes. Higher up, thick moss covers the forest and the mood changes completely.
Aeta Campsite is described as about 2 hours above the last waterfall. Close to a stream, it has room for roughly a dozen to twenty tents, which gives the trip a true night-in-the-mountains feel.
Sugo, Naliwatan, and the main summit form one range, and each peak is said to differ in height and character. Some operators run longer routes that start at Peak 1 and cover several peaks.
Pitcher plants are said to grow near the summit. Many reports also mention snakes, centipedes, and rats, which adds to the feeling of an untouched mountain.
Some reports add a stop at nearby waterfalls or hot springs after coming down. Masongsong Pool and Mainit Hot Springs are mentioned, but confirm locally whether they are open.

items.title: Two-day summit climb
items.subtitle: Start at Sampao, one night at Aeta Campsite

children.text: Travel from Tacloban or Ormoc to Naval on Biliran Island. Buy snacks, water, and food at the Naval market, and take a motorcycle taxi to Sampao if needed.
Sign in and pay the registration fee at the village registration area. A guide is assigned here, and several sources list the guide fee at about
per day.
You pass Sampawan Falls and reach Ulan-Ulan Falls. A hiking blog says it took about
1.5 hours
to 2 hours from the entrance to this fall. Lunch is usually eaten nearby.
Pass Recoletos Falls and Nomads Falls, follow the river, and finish with a steep, muddy climb to Aeta Campsite. According to one report, it took
about 5 hours
from the falls to camp. Pitch your tent and cook dinner before dark.
Wake early, eat a light breakfast, and head for the summit. Reports vary widely on the climb from camp to the summit, from
45 minutes to 2 hours
After photos at the summit, return to camp, pack up, and go back down to Sampao by the same trail. The descent is reported at
about 4~5 hours
, and one source mentions a shortcut that bypasses the waterfalls.
Travel from Sampao to Naval, then back to Tacloban or Ormoc. Check the last vehicle departure times in advance.
Times differ greatly between trip reports. A late start on day 1 can mean reaching camp after dark, so begin the trek in the morning.
Direct flights operate from Manila to Tacloban (TAC). The first flight reportedly arrives early enough to start the climb that morning.
Schedules vary by airline, so check the latest timetable.
Most trip reports use Tacloban or Ormoc as the base and enter Biliran through Naval.
Take a van (V-hire) or bus from Tacloban across the Biliran bridge to Naval. One report took about
3 hours
from Tacloban to Sampao.

From Sampao to the start of the trail you can walk or ride the same motorcycle. It is convenient to arrange the guide and transport together. Renting a van for your schedule is another option, and a larger group can split the cost.

The trail follows waterfalls and streams, so on rainy days the water rises and becomes dangerous. Biliran and Leyte lie on the eastern seaboard, where rain is frequent year-round and is reported to be heaviest from November to January. Trip reports after several days of rain often describe fierce waterfalls and slippery trails.

March to May is generally said to be drier and better for hiking, but weather differs each year, so always check the forecast before leaving. In wet weather the streams above the falls can swell too much to cross, and guides may refuse to go on.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Rising water makes stream crossings dangerous. Consider postponing.
The easiest time to climb. Hot by day, chilly at the summit.
Do not climb when a typhoon warning is issued. The summit is foggy in rain.

There is no lodging on the mountain; the usual practice is to pitch a tent at Aeta Campsite. Bring your own tent, sleeping bag, and rain cover, or ask locally whether a guide can arrange rentals. Water is easy to find because a stream runs nearby, but bring your own way to purify it.

Most hikers cook for themselves, buying rice, canned food, noodles, and snacks in advance at the Naval market or a convenience store. Sampao itself is said to have only small sari-sari shops. Before and after the climb you can stay in Naval and eat at local restaurants, though which places are open changes by season, so confirm locally.
Hiring a guide in Sampao and climbing together is the usual practice. It is safer not to climb alone.
Start as early in the morning as you can. Some trip reports describe groups that started late and reached camp after dark.
Bring a waterproof pack cover, a change of clothes, and spare socks. Clothes get wet easily from the waterfalls and streams.
Mossy rocks are very slippery. Wear hiking shoes with good soles or good grip.
Bring swimwear and a towel to relax in the waterfall pools. However, one report warns that jumping into water right after a long trek is dangerous, so cool down first.
Bring plenty of batteries and a power bank. Signal can be weak or absent in the mountains.
Check current fees and registration rules in advance with the Almeria barangay office or a local guide. Most fees in this entry come from sources several years old.
Postpone the climb right after rain or during a typhoon warning, because the waterfalls and streams become dangerous. If the guide advises stopping, follow that advice.
Several sources report snakes on the trail. Do not grab stick-like objects in the grass.
In the stream sections, climbers have been stung by bees (one group reported disturbing a nest and running) or hurt in slips. Walk slowly and stay behind your guide.
The section just below the summit is steep, with mud and tree roots, and is tiring. Do not push yourself if you lack the stamina.
The summit area can be foggy and chilly. Bring a windbreaker and spare clothes.
Information from commercial programs and operators is dated. Always verify contact details and prices again.
An island northwest of Biliran, suited to adding a beach rest to the trip after the climb. Boat options and travel times change by season, so confirm locally.
A sandbar island off Palompon in northwest Leyte, a candidate when you want to add a sea outing after the climb.
The nearest air gateway city for this climb, good for a day's stay before or after the hike for meals and shopping.
The city travelers from Cebu pass through by boat, and the vans to Naval leave from here.
